title: If you are able
hook: Hajj is due once in a lifetime on those with health, means and safety (3:97)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the fast with two joys, the one at the table and the one still waited for. Did you eat a first bite slowly? Today, a new part: the pilgrimage. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

Three times a man asks the same question, and twice the answer is silence. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has just told the people that Allah has made the pilgrimage a duty for them, so they should go on pilgrimage. The man calls out: every year, Messenger of Allah? The Prophet says nothing. The man asks again. Silence. He asks a third time. And the answer, kept in Sahih Muslim, is not the one the man expected. If I said yes, it would become a duty, and you would not be able to do it. Today, istita'ah.

First, the verse. Surah three of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither." The House is the Kaaba in Mecca. And the duty comes with its own condition already attached: for the one who can find a way. Second, the word. Istita'ah means being able, having the capacity. It's the word jurists use for that condition. The duty of Hajj isn't on everyone in general. It's on the one who is able. Third, what able means. Scholars of the schools spell it out, and they differ on some details, but the broad shape is health enough to make the journey, the means to pay for it without leaving one's family short, and a road safe enough to travel. A person missing one of those isn't failing a duty. For them, it isn't yet due. Fourth, how often. That's where the man's question comes in. Some readers hear the Prophet's silence as a mercy. He doesn't add to what's been asked. And the report goes on: he tells the people to leave him be as long as he leaves them be, and to do what they're commanded as far as they're able. Scholars read it this way: the duty is once in a lifetime, for those who can, and anything more is voluntary. Put together, the condition is part of the pillar itself. Hajj waits until a person can go. For some, that comes early. For some, it takes a lifetime of saving. For some, it never becomes possible, and they keep the intention.
screen: `FOR HIM WHO CAN FIND A WAY.` · `ISTITA'AH: BEING ABLE.` · `HEALTH, MEANS, A SAFE ROAD.` · `ONCE IN A LIFETIME.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for your chance, or hold the hope. Settle, and breathe slowly. If you're Muslim and you pray, you can ask, in your own words, for the means and the health to make the journey one day, or give thanks if you already have. If not, think of one journey you've long wanted to make, one that matters to you, and notice what stands between you and it: health, money, time, safety. No need to solve it. Just see it clearly. The bell holds the time.
Istita'ah. Being able: the condition the Qur'an sets on Hajj, for the one who can find a way. Today's word.
Your line: once, if able. Today, notice one thing you're able to do now that you once couldn't, and do it. Tomorrow: umrah and Hajj. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims who have the health, money and safe passage go on Hajj once in their lives; some save for years, and those who cannot go keep the intention and sometimes, by their school's rules, send someone in their place.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. a man asks, three times, whether Hajj is due every year. what do you answer?
options: if I said yes, it would become a duty, and you would not be able.
only in the years you feel ready.
fork.reveal: he answers that saying yes would make it a duty no one could keep. once in a lifetime, for those who are able.
